demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I remind myself it could have been worse
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette: Vikram was forty-two years old, a tax inspector for the state, when he came home one rainy November evening and, for a split second, looked down at his phone while waiting at a red light. He saw the pedestrian too late. The man was crossing with the walk signal, and Vikram’s sedan struck him at low speed, but the impact threw the man sideways into the curb. He died of a subdural hematoma three hours later. Vikram was not charged—the investigation concluded it was a tragic accident, no impairment, no recklessness—but that conclusion meant nothing to him. What he carried was the sound: the dull thud against the bumper, and then the wet, scraping noise of fabric on asphalt. Those sounds replayed in his head without warning, often in the middle of a quiet moment at his desk. He would be reviewing a return, and suddenly he would hear it again—the thud, the scrape—with a clarity that made his hands go cold. Yet the rest of the event was fragmented. He could see the man’s coat, a dark blue raincoat, but he could not picture the man’s face. He could remember the exact time on the dashboard clock—7:14 PM—but not whether he had braked before or after the impact. Some moments were impossibly sharp; others were simply gone. This unevenness troubled Vikram deeply. He had come to believe that the gaps in his memory were proof that he was hiding from the truth, that his mind was protecting him from something so terrible he could not bear to see it. And if he could not bear to see it, he reasoned, then he was a coward on top of everything else. He told himself he deserved to suffer for what he had done, and he made sure he did. Whenever a pleasant moment arose—his wife laughing at a show, a colleague complimenting his work—he would silently remind himself that it could have been worse, that the man’s family had it far worse, and that he had no right to feel anything but guilt. He tried to suppress the memories, pushing them down with brute force, but the suppression only made the auditory intrusions sharper when they broke through. The triggers were everywhere. Every car he saw pulling away from a crosswalk made his stomach drop. Driving became a series of small, electric jolts of fear. He started taking back roads to avoid intersections. Then a colleague mentioned a funeral, and Vikram felt his throat close—he saw the raincoat again, imagined the man’s family standing at a grave, and he nearly excused himself from the room. Talking about the event itself was impossible; when his wife gently asked what had happened, he said he did not want to discuss it and left the table. The more he avoided these triggers, the more they seemed to multiply. He began to feel that the world was a place where catastrophe could arrive from a moment’s distraction, and that he was permanently marked by his failure to protect a stranger. He felt humiliated, not by any public shame—no one blamed him—but by the private knowledge that he had been the one looking at his phone. That humiliation became a lens through which he saw his memory. He would replay the partial fragments and think, *You are only remembering what lets you feel sorry for yourself. The real truth is worse.* And so the gaps in his memory became evidence of his moral failing, and his moral failing made the gaps feel more sinister, more deliberate. He started working longer hours, staying at the office until the cleaning staff came through, because the routine of tax forms was numbing. But even there, the triggers found him. A client’s file mentioned a car accident settlement, and Vikram had to excuse himself to the restroom, where he stood gripping the sink and hearing the scrape of fabric on asphalt. He would then tell himself, *You deserve this. It could have been worse. You deserve every second of this.* That thought loop—trigger, suppression, self-punishment, more trigger—tightened over months. He stopped driving entirely. His wife drove him to work. He stopped attending family gatherings where anyone might mention a recent death. He stopped talking about the accident, even to her, because every conversation felt like a trap that would lead back to the raincoat and the dashboard clock. What finally brought him to seek help was a single moment: he was standing in the grocery store aisle, staring at a display of rain jackets, and he could not move. He stood there for ten minutes, frozen, until a store employee asked if he needed assistance. Vikram walked out without buying anything, got into the passenger seat of his wife’s car, and told her he needed to see someone. What frightened him most was the thought that this would never stop—that he would spend the rest of his life trapped in a loop of sound and silence, forever hearing a thud he could not undo.
